title: EXPLORE SOFTWARE OR TOOL SUBSCRIPTION WITH CHATGPT
content:
Subscription software works when a customer has a problem worth continuing to solve. The first question is not which programming language to use. It is what useful job the tool keeps doing for the customer.

THE RECURRING PROBLEM COMES FIRST
A tool is a stronger subscription candidate when the customer's need keeps returning. A one-time task may fit a one-off tool better unless continued access creates additional value.

KEEP THE FIRST VERSION SMALL ENOUGH TO REASON ABOUT
Identify the user, recurring job, and smallest useful set of functions. You do not need to design an entire software company here.

ONGOING COSTS MATTER
Hosting, APIs, AI usage, support, maintenance, security, and third-party services can create recurring costs just as customer payments recur. They belong in feasibility research.

MINIMUM CONCEPT EXAMPLE
Too broad: "I want to make an app for contractors."
More useful: "I want to explore a simple subscription tool that helps small residential contractors turn job notes into customer-ready project summaries."

The second statement still leaves technical and market questions unanswered, but it identifies a customer, recurring job, and reason software might be useful.

KEEP THE FIRST SOFTWARE IDEA SMALL ENOUGH TO UNDERSTAND

A subscription tool does not need to begin as a giant platform. Start with a recurring job a particular customer needs done and ask what the smallest useful tool would have to accomplish.

The interview should separate essential functionality from features that merely sound impressive. It should also test whether the problem really recurs. If the customer needs the result once, a one-off tool or service may be a better fit than a subscription.

You are choosing a business concept here, not writing a technical specification or deciding the entire software stack.

FOLLOW A SIMPLE SOFTWARE SUBSCRIPTION

Imagine a tool that helps independent cleaners create estimates from room counts, service type, and selected add-ons.

A cleaner creates an account and pays $15 for access this month. During the month, she uses the tool for several customer estimates. At the end of the month, she has not "used up" the software. She pays another $15 because she expects to need the functionality again next month.

That recurring job is the foundation of the subscription.

Now imagine she only needs the tool once to calculate a single startup price list that never changes. Continued monthly access becomes harder to justify. The exact same software could be technically capable of charging monthly while being poorly matched to a subscription model.

WHY SOFTWARE SUBSCRIPTIONS CREATE ONGOING RESPONSIBILITY

Customers are not only buying the code that existed on signup day. They are relying on continued access. Hosting, maintenance, bugs, security, integrations, customer support, changing external systems, and ongoing usefulness can all become part of keeping the promise.

You do not need to understand how to build all of that yet. You do need to decide whether you want a business where the product remains an ongoing system rather than a finished file.

WHAT YOU SHOULD DECIDE HERE

Do not ask first, "Could I build an app?"

Ask, "Is there a repeated job valuable enough that someone would want continued access to a tool that performs it?"

If yes, then explore how simple the first useful version could be and what building or maintaining it would require.

A software subscription can be appealing when the same functioning system serves many customers repeatedly. It becomes less appealing if the idea requires constant custom work for every customer or if the problem is solved permanently after one use.

Your job here is to decide whether repeated functionality is the product you want to own.

HOW TO USE THIS
Use the prompt below to turn this branch into your version of the business. Answer the questions honestly, ask for clarification when you need it, and do not treat external facts as verified just because ChatGPT mentions them.

WHAT THIS INTERVIEW SHOULD PRODUCE

By the end, you should have a repeated customer job, a proposed tool that performs it, a reason continued access could remain valuable, and a realistic list of build and maintenance unknowns.

ChatGPT should search for the smallest useful version before proposing a large software platform.

It should distinguish what could be explored conceptually from what requires whether it can actually be made or built work, security review, cost research, or other outside expertise.

COPY & PASTE INTO CHATGPT

During the interview:
- Ask one question at a time unless a small group of tightly related questions is genuinely easier to answer together.
- Use my answers before deciding what to ask next. Do not run through a generic questionnaire when an answer makes a question irrelevant.
- If I say "I don't know," help me identify what I need to decide or research. Do not silently invent an answer for me.
- Explain unfamiliar business terms in plain language when they first become relevant.
- Separate assumptions from facts that require outside verification.
- Do not turn this into a marketing or customer-acquisition plan unless the purpose of this specific interview requires it.
- When you have enough information, stop interviewing me and give me the requested conclusion, including the important unknowns and next research questions.
Ask me one question at a time unless a small group of closely related questions would be easier to answer together. If I say I don't know, help me identify what I would need to decide or research instead of inventing an answer for me.

Interview me about a software or tool subscription idea at the business-concept level. Ask who the customer is, what recurring problem they have, what job the tool would perform, why continued access is useful, what alternatives exist, and the minimum functionality that would make it valuable.

Ask about my technical resources and constraints, and help me consider build, contractor, existing-platform, or no-code possibilities only at a high level. Explore ongoing costs, support, and what would make customers stay subscribed.

Do not claim whether it can actually be made or built or market demand. Flag development estimates, security, privacy, data handling, third-party APIs, platform terms, legal obligations, and demand for independent verification.

End with a specific tool concept and feasibility questions.

NEXT → PDF 46 if clear; PDF 32 for another subscription type.

While interviewing me, follow these rules:

Stay at business-concept level unless the user explicitly wants technical implementation later. The goal here is to determine whether a recurring problem could support a useful tool.

Do not inflate the minimum product into a large feature list. Push toward the smallest useful job.

At the end, give me:
- Customer
- Recurring problem
- Core job of the tool
- Minimum useful functionality
- Reason for continued payment
- Technical/resource unknowns
- Ongoing-cost questions
- Specific subscription-tool direction
